text.en: Ravi rubbed a plastic comb on his hair and it picked up tiny paper bits. "Electric charge!" said his teacher.

Matter contains positive and negative charges. An atom that gains extra electrons becomes a negative ion. One electron has charge approximately minus one point six times ten to the power minus nineteen coulombs. Its magnitude is the elementary charge. Add positive and negative contributions to find the net charge. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract, and this force is the electric force.
Electric current is the rate at which charge flows past a point in a circuit. By convention it is taken as the flow of positive charge, called conventional current. A cell transfers energy to charges in a circuit. Its electromotive force is the energy it supplies per unit of charge passing through the source. Potential difference is V = W / q.
Resistance is the opposition a component offers to the flow of current. One ohm is the resistance when a potential difference of one volt drives one ampere. Good conductors have low resistance and resistors are components made to provide resistance. Electric current has heating, magnetic and chemical effects, and electricity can be dangerous if it is handled carelessly.

A neutral atom has equal proton and electron counts. When it loses an electron, it has one more positive charge than negative charge and becomes a positive ion.

board.text: Lose one electron → charge becomes more positive

text.en: A charged comb can attract small neutral paper pieces. Charge in the paper shifts slightly so the side nearer the comb feels a stronger attraction.

board.text: Attraction can occur with a neutral object

text.en: Adding equal positive and negative charges gives zero net charge. Two positive elementary charges and one negative elementary charge add to one positive elementary charge.
Electric force can act even when objects do not touch. An electric field describes the force that a small positive test charge would feel at different positions.

board.text: Field direction follows force on a positive test charge

text.en: In a field sketch around a positive point charge, arrows point outward. Around a negative point charge, arrows point inward. These arrows describe the field rather than the paths of all moving charges.
Electric potential describes electric potential energy per unit charge at a point, relative to an agreed reference. A difference in potential compares two points.

board.text: Potential: energy per charge relative to reference

text.en: If six coulombs of charge pass a point in three seconds, the average current is two amperes. An ampere is one coulomb per second.
In the outside wires of a battery circuit, conventional current points from the battery’s positive side toward its negative side. Electrons in the metal drift the other way.

board.text: Conventional current and electron drift have opposite directions

text.en: A cell can have a voltage across its terminals while a switch is open. With a break in the conducting path, no sustained current through the lamp can flow.

board.text: Potential difference can exist in an open circuit

text.en: A battery may combine more than one cell. Its role is to transfer energy, while charges already present in the circuit move through a complete conducting path.
One volt means a difference of one joule per coulomb. If a device transfers twelve joules as four coulombs pass through it, the potential difference is three volts.
Keep electromotive force and terminal potential difference distinct. In the simple ideal-cell model they are equal. A real cell’s terminal voltage can drop when it supplies current.

board.text: Ideal cell: terminal voltage equals emf

text.en: An ammeter measures current through part of a circuit. Put the ammeter in series in the same branch you want to measure, so the measured current passes through the instrument.
A voltmeter compares electric potential at two points. Across a lamp, each lead goes to one terminal, so the meter sits in a separate parallel branch.

Resistance describes how strongly a component opposes current. One ohm corresponds to one volt across a component carrying one ampere. In practice, resistance can depend on temperature and the material.
A circuit diagram uses symbols to show connections. Two drawings can look different but describe the same circuit if the components connect to the same points.
In a simple series circuit there is only one path, so the current is the same through each component. In a branched circuit the incoming current divides between the branches.
Current can warm a resistor. It can also produce a magnetic field near a wire. The movement of a nearby compass needle in a teacher demonstration gives evidence of that field.
In some conducting liquids, charged ions carry current and chemical changes can occur at electrodes. An industrial example is coating an object with a thin layer of metal.

board.text: In liquids, ions can carry charge

text.en: In direct current, the direction of current stays the same. In alternating current, the direction changes repeatedly. A small battery circuit uses direct current.
Use only a teacher-provided low-voltage battery kit for classroom measurements. Have the teacher check the connections with the switch open and keep classroom circuits away from wall sockets.
When a circuit problem gives charge and time, calculate current. When it gives energy and charge, calculate potential difference. Check whether the resulting unit should be ampere or volt.

problem.en: A charge of 6 C passes through a lamp in 3 s and transfers 18 J of energy. Find the average current and the potential difference.

text.en: Divide six coulombs by three seconds.

why.en: Charge per second gives an average current of two amperes.

text.en: Divide eighteen joules by six coulombs.

why.en: Energy per charge gives a potential difference of three volts.

prompt.en: A friend says Current flows only in metals as electrons. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Conventional current is taken as the flow of positive charge.
Charges can also move in liquids and gases.

points.en: Charge of an electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
